Source A (primary source)
The Book of Tea, I. The Cup of Humanity (opening)
Kakuzo Okakura (writing in English for Western readers), 1906 (New York: Fox, Duffield & Co.). Project Gutenberg eBook #769. Reuse: public domain in the United States (published before 1929). excerpted (1 segment); whitespace normalized; no wording changed.
Context: Kakuzo Okakura was a Japanese art scholar who wrote this book in English in 1906 for American readers.

"Tea began as a medicine and grew into a beverage. In China, in the eighth century, it entered the realm of poetry as one of the polite amusements. The fifteenth century saw Japan ennoble it into a religion of aestheticism--Teaism. Teaism is a cult founded on the adoration of the beautiful among the sordid facts of everyday existence. It inculcates purity and harmony, the mystery of mutual charity, the romanticism of the social order. It is essentially a worship of the Imperfect, as it is a tender attempt to accomplish something possible in this impossible thing we know as life. The Philosophy of Tea is not mere aestheticism in the ordinary acceptance of the term, for it expresses conjointly with ethics and religion our whole point of view about man and nature. It is hygiene, for it enforces cleanliness; it is economics, for it shows comfort in simplicity rather than in the complex and costly; it is moral geometry, inasmuch as it defines our sense of proportion to the universe. It represents the true spirit of Eastern democracy by making all its votaries aristocrats in taste. The long isolation of Japan from the rest of the world, so conducive to introspection, has been highly favourable to the development of Teaism."

———

Source B (primary source)
Bushido, the Soul of Japan (excerpt on the origin of the warrior code)
Inazo Nitobe (Japanese author writing in English for Western readers), 1900 (Philadelphia: Leeds & Biddle). Project Gutenberg eBook #12096. Reuse: public domain in the United States (published before 1929). excerpted (2 segments joined by [...]); whitespace normalized; no wording changed.
Context: Inazo Nitobe was a Japanese educator who published this book in English in 1900 to explain the code of the warrior class of Japan's feudal age to Western readers.

"Bushido, then, is the code of moral principles which the knights were required or instructed to observe. It is not a written code; at best it consists of a few maxims handed down from mouth to mouth or coming from the pen of some well-known warrior or savant. More frequently it is a code unuttered and unwritten, possessing all the more the powerful sanction of veritable deed, and of a law written on the fleshly tablets of the heart. It was founded not on the creation of one brain, however able, or on the life of a single personage, however renowned. It was an organic growth of decades and centuries of military career. It, perhaps, fills the same position in the history of ethics that the English Constitution does in political history; yet it has had nothing to compare with the Magna Charta or the Habeas Corpus Act. True, early in the seventeenth century Military Statutes (Buké Hatto) were promulgated; but their thirteen short articles were taken up mostly with marriages, castles, leagues, etc., and didactic regulations were but meagerly touched upon. We cannot, therefore, point out any definite time and place and say, “Here is its fountain head.” Only as it attains consciousness in the feudal age, its origin, in respect to time, may be identified with feudalism. [...] As in England the political institutions of feudalism may be said to date from the Norman Conquest, so we may say that in Japan its rise was simultaneous with the ascendency of Yoritomo, late in the twelfth century."

items.stem: Which of the following best describes a main idea shared by Source A and Source B?

options.text: Both trace the traditions to formal written codes issued by Japanese rulers to regulate the behavior of the elite.
options.why: Nitobe stresses that bushido is unwritten and that the Buke Hatto barely dealt with ethics. Okakura names no code at all.
options.label: reversal

options.text: Both claim that the traditions were open to all social classes rather than being limited to elites.
options.why: Okakura's talk of Eastern democracy is a figure of speech about taste, and Nitobe describes a code meant only for the knights, the warrior class.
options.label: overstated

options.text: Both argue that the traditions were borrowed from China and preserved in Japan without any significant change.
options.why: Okakura says Japan transformed tea into Teaism, and Nitobe never mentions China. Neither author describes a tradition kept unchanged.
options.label: unsupported_by_source

options.text: Both present a Japanese tradition as the product of gradual development over a long period.
options.why: Okakura traces tea from medicine to beverage to Tang poetry to fifteenth-century Teaism. Nitobe calls bushido an organic growth of decades and centuries with no single fountain head.

items.stem: The rise of feudalism that Nitobe ties to the ascendency of Yoritomo late in the twelfth century took place in the context of

options.text: the adoption of a centralized Chinese-style bureaucracy in which the emperor ruled through appointed scholar-officials
options.why: The Chinese-style reforms date to the seventh century. Yoritomo's rise moved Japan away from imperial central rule, not toward it.
options.label: wrong_period

options.why: Minamoto no Yoritomo founded the Kamakura shogunate. Real power passed to the shogun and his warrior vassals, while the imperial court in Kyoto kept mostly ceremonial authority.

items.stem: The movement of tea culture from China to Japan described in Source A was most closely connected to which development in the period c. 1200 to c. 1450?

options.text: Muslim merchants traveling the Silk Roads introduced tea to Japan as part of the spread of Sufi devotional practice
options.why: Sufism spread through Muslim trade networks in Central, South, and Southeast Asia. It played no part in bringing tea to Japan.
options.label: unrelated_development

options.text: Mongol rulers of the Yuan dynasty imposed Chinese customs on Japan after incorporating it into their empire
options.why: The Yuan never conquered Japan, so they could not have imposed customs on it.
options.label: reversal

options.text: Japanese Buddhist monks who studied in China brought back Zen teachings and tea-drinking customs
options.why: Monks such as Eisai studied in Song China and brought Chan (Zen) Buddhism and tea practices back to Japan. Zen temples then helped shape the tea culture that Okakura says Japan ennobled.
options.label: key

options.text: Portuguese merchants carried Chinese tea to Japanese ports as part of their expanding Indian Ocean trade network
options.why: The Portuguese did not reach Japan until the 1540s, long after tea culture was established there.
options.label: wrong_period

items.explanation_en:
The correct answer is "Japanese Buddhist monks who studied in China brought back Zen teachings and tea-drinking customs". Monks such as Eisai studied in Song China and brought Chan (Zen) Buddhism and tea practices back to Japan. Zen temples then helped shape the tea culture that Okakura says Japan ennobled.
"Muslim merchants traveling the Silk Roads introduced tea to Japan as part of the spread of Sufi devotional practice" is incorrect: Sufism spread through Muslim trade networks in Central, South, and Southeast Asia. It played no part in bringing tea to Japan.

facts: The Japanese monk Eisai brought Rinzai Zen from Song China to Japan in 1191 and wrote a treatise promoting tea in 1211.

design.key_evidence_in_source: Okakura places early tea culture in China and its fifteenth-century transformation in Japan, which points to cultural transmission between the two.
design.evidence_quote: The fifteenth century saw Japan ennoble it into a religion of aestheticism--Teaism.

Context: Marco Polo was a Venetian merchant who spent years in Mongol-ruled China in the 13th century; his account was written down around 1298. These passages describe policies of the Great Khan, Kublai.

"Now you must know that the Emperor sends his Messengers over all his Lands and Kingdoms and Provinces, to ascertain from his officers if the people are afflicted by any dearth through unfavourable seasons, or storms or locusts, or other like calamity; and from those who have suffered in this way no taxes are exacted for that year; nay more, he causes them to be supplied with corn of his own for food and seed. Now this is undoubtedly a great bounty on his part. And when winter comes, he causes inquiry to be made as to those who have lost their cattle, whether by murrain or other mishap, and such persons not only go scot free, but get presents of cattle. And thus, as I tell you, the Lord every year helps and fosters the people subject to him. [...] The Emperor moreover hath taken order that all the highways travelled by his messengers and the people generally should be planted with rows of great trees a few paces apart; and thus these trees are visible a long way off, and no one can miss the way by day or night. Even the roads through uninhabited tracts are thus planted, and it is the greatest possible solace to travellers. And this is done on all the ways, where it can be of service. [The Great Kaan plants these trees all the more readily, because his astrologers and diviners tell him that he who plants trees lives long.{1} But where the ground is so sandy and desert that trees will not grow, he causes other landmarks, pillars or stones, to be set up to show the way."

Context: Humboldt was a naturalist from Prussia who traveled in the Spanish colonies of South America from 1799 to 1804; this passage describes the valleys of Aragua in Venezuela.

"By felling the trees which cover the tops and the sides of mountains, men in every climate prepare at once two calamities for future generations; want of fuel and scarcity of water. Trees, by the nature of their perspiration, and the radiation from their leaves in a sky without clouds, surround themselves with an atmosphere constantly cold and misty. They affect the copiousness of springs, not, as was long believed, by a peculiar attraction for the vapours diffused through the air, but because, by sheltering the soil from the direct action of the sun, they diminish the evaporation of water produced by rain. When forests are destroyed, as they are everywhere in America by the European planters, with imprudent precipitancy, the springs are entirely dried up, or become less abundant. The beds of the rivers, remaining dry during a part of the year, are converted into torrents whenever great rains fall on the heights. As the sward and moss disappear with the brushwood from the sides of the mountains, the waters falling in rain are no longer impeded in their course; and instead of slowly augmenting the level of the rivers by progressive filtrations, they furrow, during heavy showers, the sides of the hills, bearing down the loosened soil, and forming sudden and destructive inundations. Hence it results, that the clearing of forests, the want of permanent springs, and the existence of torrents, are three phenomena closely connected together. Countries situated in opposite hemispheres, as, for example, Lombardy bordered by the Alps, and Lower Peru inclosed between the Pacific and the Cordillera of the Andes, afford striking proofs of the justness of this assertion. Till the middle of the last century, the mountains round the valleys of Aragua were covered with forests. Great trees of the families of mimosa, ceiba, and the fig-tree, shaded and spread coolness along the banks of the lake. The plain, then thinly inhabited, was filled with brushwood, interspersed with trunks of scattered trees and parasite plants, enveloped with a thick sward, less capable of emitting radiant caloric than the soil that is cultivated and consequently not sheltered from the rays of the sun. With the destruction of the trees, and the increase of the cultivation of sugar, indigo, and cotton, the springs, and all the natural supplies of the lake of Valencia, have diminished from year to year."

sources.title: My Life and Work, ch. on mass production (excerpt on the assembly line)
sources.attribution: Henry Ford with Samuel Crowther, American automobile manufacturer, 1922 (Garden City, N.Y.: Doubleday, Page). Project Gutenberg eBook #7213. Reuse: public domain in the United States (published before 1929). excerpted (2 segments joined by [...]); whitespace normalized; no wording changed.
sources.context: Henry Ford founded the Ford Motor Company in Michigan; he published this book in 1922 about the company's methods.

items.stem: The production process Ford describes in the excerpt best illustrates which of the following developments in industrial work in the early twentieth century?

options.text: The breaking of a single skilled task into many simple, repeated steps to raise output
options.why: Ford reports that one worker's complete job was spread into twenty-nine operations on a moving line, which cut assembly time. This is the division of labor and deskilling at the center of mass production.
options.label: key

options.text: The spread of the putting-out system in which merchants supplied raw materials to rural families working at home
options.why: The putting-out system belongs to early modern, pre-factory production. Ford describes centralized factory assembly in 1913 and 1914.
options.label: wrong_period

options.text: The shift of manufacturing from private firms to state ministries that set output targets for each factory
options.why: State-directed output targets describe Soviet planning. Ford was a private manufacturer describing his own company's methods.
options.label: misattributed

options.text: The revival of artisan workshops in which one craftsman built a complete product by hand for local buyers
options.why: The excerpt describes moving away from one workman doing a complete job, which is the opposite of craft production.
options.label: reversal

items.explanation_en:
The correct answer is "The breaking of a single skilled task into many simple, repeated steps to raise output". Ford reports that one worker's complete job was spread into twenty-nine operations on a moving line, which cut assembly time. This is the division of labor and deskilling at the center of mass production.
"The spread of the putting-out system in which merchants supplied raw materials to rural families working at home" is incorrect: The putting-out system belongs to early modern, pre-factory production. Ford describes centralized factory assembly in 1913 and 1914.
"The shift of manufacturing from private firms to state ministries that set output targets for each factory" is incorrect: State-directed output targets describe Soviet planning. Ford was a private manufacturer describing his own company's methods.
"The revival of artisan workshops in which one craftsman built a complete product by hand for local buyers" is incorrect: The excerpt describes moving away from one workman doing a complete job, which is the opposite of craft production.
facts: Ford Motor Company introduced the moving assembly line at its Highland Park, Michigan, plant in 1913.
Mass production based on dividing work into simple repeated tasks spread in early twentieth-century industry.

design.key_evidence_in_source: Ford says one worker's full magneto assembly was split into twenty-nine operations, which cut the time per unit.
design.evidence_quote: What he did alone was then spread into twenty-nine operations; that cut down the assembly time to thirteen minutes, ten seconds.

items.stem: Which of the following claims does Ford make in the excerpt?

options.text: New methods should be installed across all plants at once, before any small trial could prove them
options.why: Ford says the company tries everything in a little way first and must know a new method is better before acting drastically.
options.label: reversal

options.text: The moving line was an entirely original invention with no model in any earlier American industry
options.why: Ford says the idea came from the overhead trolley that Chicago meatpackers used.
options.label: reversal

options.text: Dividing the magneto job among many workers on a moving line cut the time needed per unit
options.why: Ford states that assembly time fell from about twenty minutes to thirteen minutes, ten seconds, then to seven minutes and finally five minutes after the work was divided and the line adjusted.
options.label: key

options.text: Skilled workers who completed whole assemblies alone remained the most efficient way to build parts
options.why: Ford argues the reverse. A single workman took about twenty minutes per assembly, far longer than the line.
options.label: reversal

items.explanation_en:
The correct answer is "Dividing the magneto job among many workers on a moving line cut the time needed per unit". Ford states that assembly time fell from about twenty minutes to thirteen minutes, ten seconds, then to seven minutes and finally five minutes after the work was divided and the line adjusted.
"New methods should be installed across all plants at once, before any small trial could prove them" is incorrect: Ford says the company tries everything in a little way first and must know a new method is better before acting drastically.
"The moving line was an entirely original invention with no model in any earlier American industry" is incorrect: Ford says the idea came from the overhead trolley that Chicago meatpackers used.
"Skilled workers who completed whole assemblies alone remained the most efficient way to build parts" is incorrect: Ford argues the reverse. A single workman took about twenty minutes per assembly, far longer than the line.
facts: Ford's first moving assembly line experiment was on the flywheel magneto in 1913.

design.key_evidence_in_source: Ford gives falling assembly times after the job was split into operations and the line's height and speed were adjusted.
design.evidence_quote: Further experimenting with the speed that the work should move at cut the time down to five minutes.

items.stem: Ford's account of the assembly line is best understood in the context of which broader development of the period c. 1900 to 1930?

options.text: The Meiji government's founding of state-owned factories to build Japanese industry and military strength
options.why: Meiji state industrialization took place in the late nineteenth century in Japan, not at a private American firm in the 1910s.
options.label: wrong_period

options.text: Wartime mobilization in which European governments took control of factories to supply munitions for the front
options.why: Ford's line began in April 1913, before the First World War started in 1914, and it was a private American effort, not European state mobilization.
options.label: wrong_period

options.text: The New Deal programs that used federal spending and public works to fight unemployment during the Depression
options.why: The New Deal began in 1933, after the period named and long after the 1913 to 1914 events Ford describes.
options.label: wrong_period

options.text: The rise of the United States as a leading industrial power producing goods for mass consumption
options.why: Ford's line in 1913 and 1914 was part of American industrial growth based on mass-produced consumer goods such as the Model T, and this growth helped make the United States a leading economic power after 1900.
options.label: key

items.explanation_en:
The correct answer is "The rise of the United States as a leading industrial power producing goods for mass consumption". Ford's line in 1913 and 1914 was part of American industrial growth based on mass-produced consumer goods such as the Model T, and this growth helped make the United States a leading economic power after 1900.
"The Meiji government's founding of state-owned factories to build Japanese industry and military strength" is incorrect: Meiji state industrialization took place in the late nineteenth century in Japan, not at a private American firm in the 1910s.
"Wartime mobilization in which European governments took control of factories to supply munitions for the front" is incorrect: Ford's line began in April 1913, before the First World War started in 1914, and it was a private American effort, not European state mobilization.
"The New Deal programs that used federal spending and public works to fight unemployment during the Depression" is incorrect: The New Deal began in 1933, after the period named and long after the 1913 to 1914 events Ford describes.
facts: Ford introduced the Model T in 1908 and the moving assembly line in 1913.
By the early twentieth century the United States had become the world's leading industrial economy.
The New Deal began in 1933.

design.key_evidence_in_source: The dates 1913 and 1914 and the American firm in the credit and context lines place the account in early twentieth-century American industrial expansion.
design.evidence_quote: Along about April 1, 1913, we first tried the experiment of an assembly line.

items.stem: Which of the following later developments most clearly shows the spread of the production methods described in the excerpt beyond the United States?

options.text: Soviet planners in the 1930s adopting American assembly line techniques in new automobile and tractor plants
options.why: During the Five-Year Plans the Soviet state brought in American methods. One example is a 1929 agreement with Ford to help build an automobile plant at Nizhny Novgorod, which carried the moving line into Soviet industry.
options.label: key

options.text: British factory owners in the early nineteenth century adopting steam-powered looms in textile mills across the Lancashire region
options.why: This mechanization came about a century before Ford's 1913 line, so it cannot be a later spread of his methods.
options.label: wrong_period

options.text: Mexican president Lazaro Cardenas redistributing large estates to peasant communities and nationalizing foreign-owned oil in the 1930s
options.why: Land reform and oil nationalization concern ownership of resources, not the organization of factory assembly work.
options.label: unrelated_development

options.text: Gandhi's campaign in the 1920s and 1930s urging Indians to spin and weave their own cloth by hand instead of buying British textiles
options.why: Gandhi promoted hand spinning as an alternative to mechanized factory production, the opposite of Ford's methods.
options.label: reversal

items.explanation_en:
The correct answer is "Soviet planners in the 1930s adopting American assembly line techniques in new automobile and tractor plants". During the Five-Year Plans the Soviet state brought in American methods. One example is a 1929 agreement with Ford to help build an automobile plant at Nizhny Novgorod, which carried the moving line into Soviet industry.
"British factory owners in the early nineteenth century adopting steam-powered looms in textile mills across the Lancashire region" is incorrect: This mechanization came about a century before Ford's 1913 line, so it cannot be a later spread of his methods.
"Mexican president Lazaro Cardenas redistributing large estates to peasant communities and nationalizing foreign-owned oil in the 1930s" is incorrect: Land reform and oil nationalization concern ownership of resources, not the organization of factory assembly work.
"Gandhi's campaign in the 1920s and 1930s urging Indians to spin and weave their own cloth by hand instead of buying British textiles" is incorrect: Gandhi promoted hand spinning as an alternative to mechanized factory production, the opposite of Ford's methods.
facts: The Soviet First Five-Year Plan began in 1928.
In 1929 the Soviet Union signed an agreement with Ford to help build an automobile plant at Nizhny Novgorod.

design.key_evidence_in_source: The question is anchored to Ford's description of the moving line he says was the first of its kind, a method later copied abroad.
design.evidence_quote: I believe that this was the first moving line ever installed.

items.stem: In the decade between the 1910 and 1920 figures in the table, which development killed tens of millions of people worldwide without reversing long-term population growth?

options.text: The famine caused by the collectivization policies of the Great Leap Forward
options.why: The Great Leap Forward famine happened in China from 1959 to 1961, after the last year in the table.
options.label: wrong_period

options.text: The Soviet famine in Ukraine that followed forced collectivization
options.why: The famine in Ukraine (the Holodomor) took place in 1932 to 1933, not in the 1910s.
options.label: wrong_period

options.text: The spread of bubonic plague across Afro-Eurasia trade routes
options.why: The Black Death struck Afro-Eurasia in the mid-1300s, centuries before this table begins.
options.label: wrong_period

options.text: The influenza pandemic of 1918 to 1919
options.why: The 1918 to 1919 influenza pandemic killed tens of millions worldwide, yet world population was still larger in 1920 than in 1910 and kept growing afterward.
options.label: key

items.explanation_en:
The correct answer is "The influenza pandemic of 1918 to 1919". The 1918 to 1919 influenza pandemic killed tens of millions worldwide, yet world population was still larger in 1920 than in 1910 and kept growing afterward.
"The famine caused by the collectivization policies of the Great Leap Forward" is incorrect: The Great Leap Forward famine happened in China from 1959 to 1961, after the last year in the table.
"The Soviet famine in Ukraine that followed forced collectivization" is incorrect: The famine in Ukraine (the Holodomor) took place in 1932 to 1933, not in the 1910s.
"The spread of bubonic plague across Afro-Eurasia trade routes" is incorrect: The Black Death struck Afro-Eurasia in the mid-1300s, centuries before this table begins.
facts: The influenza pandemic of 1918 to 1919 killed tens of millions of people worldwide.
The Great Leap Forward famine took place in China from 1959 to 1961.
The Soviet famine in Ukraine happened in 1932 to 1933.

items.stem: The data in the table would best support which of the following claims about the first half of the twentieth century?

options.text: Most of the world's population growth between 1900 and 1950 took place in South and East Asia.
options.why: The table gives only world totals, with no regional breakdown, so it cannot support a claim about where the growth happened.
options.label: unsupported_by_source

options.text: World population grew substantially even though two world wars took place.
options.why: Both the lower and upper estimates for 1950 are well above those for 1900, so the population kept growing through the wars of 1914 to 1918 and 1939 to 1945.
options.label: key

options.text: World population more than doubled between 1900 and 1950 because birth rates rose so quickly.
options.why: The estimates rise by roughly half, not by more than double. The table also gives no birth rates.
options.label: overstated

options.text: Deaths in the two world wars caused world population to shrink between 1900 and 1950.
options.why: The table shows the opposite: estimates for 1950 are much higher than estimates for 1900.
options.label: reversal

items.explanation_en:
The correct answer is "World population grew substantially even though two world wars took place.". Both the lower and upper estimates for 1950 are well above those for 1900, so the population kept growing through the wars of 1914 to 1918 and 1939 to 1945.
"Most of the world's population growth between 1900 and 1950 took place in South and East Asia." is incorrect: The table gives only world totals, with no regional breakdown, so it cannot support a claim about where the growth happened.
"World population more than doubled between 1900 and 1950 because birth rates rose so quickly." is incorrect: The estimates rise by roughly half, not by more than double. The table also gives no birth rates.
"Deaths in the two world wars caused world population to shrink between 1900 and 1950." is incorrect: The table shows the opposite: estimates for 1950 are much higher than estimates for 1900.
facts: World War I lasted from 1914 to 1918 and World War II from 1939 to 1945.
World population is estimated to have grown from roughly 1.6 to 1.7 billion in 1900 to roughly 2.5 billion in 1950.

design.key_evidence_in_source: The 1950 lower and upper estimates are both well above the 1900 estimates, even though the period includes both world wars.
design.evidence_quote: summary lower and upper estimates, millions

items.stem: The overall trend shown in the table is best explained in the context of which broader development of the period?

options.text: Fertility in most industrialized societies falling below the level needed to replace each generation
options.why: Fertility below replacement level is a late twentieth century trend that slows population growth. It does not explain the growth shown here.
options.label: reversal

options.text: Higher living standards across Africa and Asia that followed the end of European colonial rule
options.why: Most decolonization happened after 1945, mainly after 1950, so it cannot explain growth that began in 1900.
options.label: wrong_period

options.text: Large harvest gains from high-yield seeds and chemical fertilizers of the Green Revolution
options.why: The Green Revolution spread mainly from the 1960s on, after the period the table covers.
options.label: wrong_period

options.text: Falling death rates as public health measures and medicine spread
options.why: Sanitation, vaccination, better medical knowledge, and by the 1940s antibiotics such as penicillin lowered death rates. Population grew because fewer people died, while birth rates stayed high in many regions.
options.label: key

items.explanation_en:
The correct answer is "Falling death rates as public health measures and medicine spread". Sanitation, vaccination, better medical knowledge, and by the 1940s antibiotics such as penicillin lowered death rates. Population grew because fewer people died, while birth rates stayed high in many regions.
"Fertility in most industrialized societies falling below the level needed to replace each generation" is incorrect: Fertility below replacement level is a late twentieth century trend that slows population growth. It does not explain the growth shown here.
"Higher living standards across Africa and Asia that followed the end of European colonial rule" is incorrect: Most decolonization happened after 1945, mainly after 1950, so it cannot explain growth that began in 1900.
"Large harvest gains from high-yield seeds and chemical fertilizers of the Green Revolution" is incorrect: The Green Revolution spread mainly from the 1960s on, after the period the table covers.
facts: Penicillin became widely used in the 1940s.
The Green Revolution in agriculture spread mainly from the 1960s.
Most African and Asian colonies gained independence after 1945.

design.key_evidence_in_source: The estimates rise steadily from 1900 to 1950, which fits a period when death rates were falling.
design.evidence_quote: Estimated world population, 1900-1950

items.stem: Which of the following developments in the second half of the twentieth century most directly continued the trend shown in the table?

options.text: Europe's share of world population grew as postwar baby booms spread across the continent.
options.why: Europe's share of world population fell after 1950 because Asia, Africa, and Latin America grew much faster.
options.label: reversal

options.text: World population stopped growing after China's one-child policy reduced births across Asia.
options.why: China's one-child policy began in 1979 and slowed growth in China, but world population kept rising quickly.
options.label: overstated

options.text: Population growth sped up, and the world passed 6 billion by about 2000.
options.why: After 1950, growth sped up rather than slowing. World population passed about 6 billion around 2000, continuing the rise shown in the table.
options.label: key

options.text: World population fell after 1950 as industrialized countries adopted family planning programs.
options.why: World population did not fall after 1950. It rose faster than before, even where birth rates declined.
options.label: reversal

items.explanation_en:
The correct answer is "Population growth sped up, and the world passed 6 billion by about 2000.". After 1950, growth sped up rather than slowing. World population passed about 6 billion around 2000, continuing the rise shown in the table.
"Europe's share of world population grew as postwar baby booms spread across the continent." is incorrect: Europe's share of world population fell after 1950 because Asia, Africa, and Latin America grew much faster.
"World population stopped growing after China's one-child policy reduced births across Asia." is incorrect: China's one-child policy began in 1979 and slowed growth in China, but world population kept rising quickly.
"World population fell after 1950 as industrialized countries adopted family planning programs." is incorrect: World population did not fall after 1950. It rose faster than before, even where birth rates declined.
facts: World population reached about 6 billion around 1999 to 2000.
China's one-child policy was introduced in 1979.
Europe's share of world population declined in the late twentieth century.

design.key_evidence_in_source: The table shows a rising trend from 1900 to 1950, which students connect to faster growth later in the century.

items.stem: In the years after 1968, this photograph was widely reproduced as an environmental symbol. That use is best understood in the context of which broader development?

options.text: The wave of decolonization in Africa, during which new states such as Ghana and Kenya gained independence from British imperial rule

items.stem: The environmental awareness that the photograph later came to symbolize most directly contributed to which of the following later developments?

"Output grew at a spectacular rate of 7 percent annually from 1977 to 1982, and by 1985, Indonesia, once the world's single largest importer of rice, was self-sufficient in its most important foodstuff. Annual production grew from about 25 million tons in the late 1970s to some 50 million tons in the mid-1990s, and it then continued at about that level thereafter. The government was intensely involved, both in stabilizing prices for urban consumers and expanding domestic output to achieve national self-sufficiency in rice production. Various government policies included the dissemination of high-yield seed varieties through the government-sponsored Mass Guidance System (Bimas) in agriculture, which also subsidized the use of fertilizer and pesticides and provided rural credit. Moreover, government intervention included control of the domestic rice price through the National Logistical Supply Organization (Bulog). Government investment in irrigation also made a significant contribution. Between 1970 and 1990, about 2.5 million hectares of existing irrigated land were rehabilitated, and irrigation was extended to another 1.2 million hectares. Expansion of food-crop cultivation slowed in the late 1980s and early 1990s as a result of ecological constraints on the intensification of cropping ratios and lower government investment in irrigation. Also, markets for agricultural commodities were depressed. Poor harvests in the mid-1990s necessitated a temporary return to rice imports, and the situation during the crisis was aggravated by repeated droughts during 1997-98 caused by El Nino. By the early years of the twenty-first century, it was apparent that the Green Revolution, started in the late 1960s, had run its course in Indonesia, but also that it had had a lasting impact on productivity in food-crop agriculture."

Context: This reference book was written for the U.S. government in the early 1990s and describes South Korean society.

"Confucianism was dominant during the last dynasty (1392-1910) but declined in force as a political philosophy following the loss of independence to Japan in 1910. Nevertheless, it retained a lingering impact on social relations even in the early 1990s. Attempts to revive Confucian ethical values, whether through the Park Chung Hee government's campaign for filial piety and loyalty in the 1970s or in occasional public seminars or newspaper editorials through the early 1990s, reflected both a decline in the practice of Confucianism as a living creed and the feeling of many South Koreans that rapid modernization and the growth of materialism had created an ethical vacuum. Population policies begun in the 1960s continued their momentum through the 1980s. Tax and medical insurance benefits for smaller families, for example, provided additional incentives for family planning in the early 1980s. The government also distributed posters, such as one featuring an attractive young couple and the slogan, "Have one child and raise it well." The effect of such efforts continued to be felt in a decline in the number of primary and middle school students; the number of middle school students alone dropped by half a million during the 1980s. The success of the family planning program was suggested by the desire of other Asian countries to send officials to Seoul for training. As the number of births per couple reached 1.9 in 1990, the population growth rate dropped to just over 0.9 percent from almost 1.6 a decade earlier, causing the Economic Planning Board to predict serious labor shortages and to authorize importing increased numbers of foreign workers. Many factories already had been compensating for such shortfalls by hiring illegal immigrants (1,000 such workers were deported in 1990), or by breaking prevailing patterns to hire married women in substantial numbers."
